opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest risk is that synthetic data can quietly narrow what a model knows rather than expand it. When you generate data from a model and train on it, you tend to amplify whatever that model already does well and lose the long tail: the rare facts, the unusual phrasings, the edge cases that real human data naturally contains. If you do that over several generations without care, you get something like model collapse. The distribution gets sharper and more homogeneous, the outputs start to look the same, and diversity just erodes.

A second risk is error propagation. A generator model makes mistakes, sometimes subtle ones, like a slightly wrong reasoning step or a confident hallucination. If you don't have a good way to verify synthetic examples, you bake those mistakes into the next model, and because they're stated fluently they're often harder to catch than noisy human data.

Third, there's a kind of self-deception in evaluation. If your synthetic training data and your benchmarks come from similar sources or similar models, you can see great numbers that don't reflect real-world capability. You're essentially grading the model on its own homework.

So the way I think about it is that synthetic data works best when there's some external grounding signal. That could be a verifier, like code that actually executes or math you can check. It could be human data mixed in to anchor the distribution, or careful filtering and diversity controls. Used that way, it's incredibly powerful, especially in domains where real data is scarce. Used naively, as just "more tokens," it can make models look better while actually making them more brittle.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest risk is that synthetic data looks like it's working right up until it isn't. When you generate data with a model and then train on it, you're essentially sampling from the model's own view of the world, and that view has a particular shape. It's smoother than reality, it's missing the long tail, and it's missing the weird stuff that real users actually do. So if you do a round of this, the model gets a little more confident and a little narrower. Do it a few more times without any grounding in real data, and you get what people call model collapse, where the distribution keeps shrinking and the model forgets the rare cases entirely.

The second risk is that you amplify your own mistakes. If the generating model has a bias or a factual error, synthetic data doesn't just preserve that, it reproduces it at scale and makes it look like consensus. A thousand examples all agreeing on something wrong is far more damaging than one, because now the student model has no signal telling it otherwise.

And the third thing, which I think gets underappreciated, is that synthetic data is only as good as the filter you put on it. Generation is cheap, verification is expensive. Where it works really well is in domains like code or math, where you can actually check whether the answer is right, so you can throw away the bad samples. Where it goes wrong is when teams generate a huge volume of plausible-sounding text with no ground truth, and then treat volume as if it were quality.

So my rule of thumb is: synthetic data is a multiplier, not a replacement. You need a real-data anchor, you need a verification mechanism, and you need to actually measure whether diversity is going up or down after each round. If you can't answer that last question, you probably shouldn't be doing it.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest risk is that you mistake more data for more information. If a model generates an answer that’s wrong, and you then train on that answer as though it were correct, you can reinforce the original mistake. And because the answer may sound very fluent and convincing, that’s not always easy to catch.

There’s also a diversity problem. A model tends to generate certain kinds of answers more often than others. If you repeatedly train on those outputs, you can lose coverage of less common cases. Your training metrics might look good, but the model becomes less useful when it encounters something outside that narrower distribution.

That doesn’t mean synthetic data is inherently bad. The question is what gives you confidence in it. Can you verify the answer? For code, for example, you can run tests, although the quality of those tests matters too. And you want to evaluate on independent, realistic examples, rather than just more data from the same generation process. Otherwise, you may be measuring how well the model imitates its own assumptions rather than whether it’s actually improving.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main risk is that you can amplify the mistakes your model already makes. If you generate a lot of data from a model and then train on it without checking the quality, you’re treating its errors and biases as if they were ground truth.

You can also lose diversity. A model tends to produce certain kinds of answers, so even if you generate millions of examples, they may cover a much narrower range than real human data. Over repeated rounds, the model can get better at imitating its own outputs while becoming less useful on real problems.

So I wouldn’t think of synthetic data as automatically good or bad. The question is: what new signal does it provide, and how do you verify that signal? For code or math, for example, you can sometimes check whether the answer works. Where verification is harder, you have to be much more careful. And ultimately, you need to evaluate on independent data that reflects the situations you actually care about.
